text: A simple machine uses one force to move one load. It can make the force bigger, but then the load moves a shorter distance.
A lever is a beam or rod that pivots on a point called a fulcrum. It is one of six simple machines. A lever makes a small input force into a greater output force.
In ancient Egypt, workers used levers to move and lift obelisks that weighed more than 100 tons.
A pulley is a wheel on an axle. A cable or belt passes over the wheel, so it can move and change direction.
Plutarch wrote that Archimedes used a system of pulleys to pull a fully loaded ship toward him, as if it were gliding through water.
An inclined plane, or ramp, helps move heavy loads over a vertical obstacle. It takes less force to move an object up a ramp than to lift it straight up. The cost is a longer distance.
Dry air is 78.08% nitrogen and 20.95% oxygen. Air also holds water vapor, on average around 1% at sea level.
Three-quarters of the air is within about 6.8 mi (11 km) of the ground. The air gets thinner the higher you go, and there is no clear edge where it ends.
The edge of space is often drawn at the Karman line, 62 mi (100 km) above the ground.
Air has weight. A column of air 1 square inch wide, from sea level to the top of the atmosphere, weighs about 14.7 lb. That is 14.7 pounds of pressure on every square inch.
Wind is air moving from a place with higher pressure to a place with lower pressure.
Up to about 62 mi (100 km) high, the air keeps the same mix of gases, because turbulence stirs it.
Water is the most abundant substance on Earth's surface. It is also the only common substance that exists as a solid, a liquid and a gas there.
Ice is an unusual solid because it is less dense than liquid water, by about 8.3%. Water expands about 9% when it freezes.
Water is at its densest at 39°F (4°C). As it gets colder and starts to freeze, it becomes less dense.
Water molecules pull on each other strongly, so water has a high surface tension. That lets razor blades and insects called water striders float on top of it.
Water is called the universal solvent and the solvent of life. It is the most studied chemical compound there is.
Ice is water frozen into a solid. It forms at or below 32°F (0°C).
The wandering albatross has the greatest wingspan of any living animal that flies, up to 11 ft (3.5 m). The great bustard is the heaviest flier, up to 46 lb (21 kg).
The longest flight ever recorded for a flying fish lasted 45 seconds.
When air flows around a wing, the air pushes on the wing. The part of that push that is at right angles to the flow is called lift. Lift usually acts upward, to work against gravity.
The Wright brothers invented and flew the first airplane in 1903. It was the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered machine heavier than air.
The first jet aircraft was the German Heinkel He 178, in 1939. The first jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, was introduced in 1952. The Boeing 707 flew for more than 60 years.
A helicopter gets its lift and thrust from spinning rotors. That lets it take off and land straight up, hover, and fly forward, backward and sideways.
Rust is a reddish-brown substance made when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Given enough time, an iron object can turn entirely to rust.
Combustion does not always make a flame. A flame is only visible when the burning substances turn to vapor.
Wood and coal do not burn as solids. First heat turns them into gases, and then those gases burn. That burning makes the heat to turn more of the solid into gas.
In 1785, Antoine Lavoisier found the correct explanation of burning. It is a reaction with oxygen from the air.
Baking soda reacts with acids. When it does, it gives off carbon dioxide gas.
Heat alone can make baking soda work as a raising agent in baking. Above 180°F (80°C), it releases carbon dioxide.
Every object with mass pulls on every other object. The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. The farther apart the objects are, the weaker the pull.
In 1915, Albert Einstein described gravity as a curving of space and time caused by mass.
In 1586, Simon Stevin dropped two cannonballs of different sizes and weights from a tower. They fell at the same rate.
Near Earth's surface, an object falling in a vacuum speeds up by about 32 ft per second, every second (9.8 m/s2). That is true no matter how heavy it is.

On August 2, 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon. They fell at the same rate and hit the ground together. On the Moon, gravity is only about one-sixth as strong as on Earth.
Air pushes back on a falling object. A skydiver reaches a top speed, called terminal velocity, of around 118 mph (190 km/h).
Atoms are extremely small, typically around 100 picometers across. More than 99.94% of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
What makes one element different from another is the number of protons in its atoms. Any atom with 11 protons is sodium. Any atom with 29 protons is copper.
Oxygen has 8 protons in each atom. So oxygen is number 8 on the list of elements.
Today 118 elements are known. The first 94 occur naturally on Earth. The other 24 only occur when scientists make them in laboratories.
In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev made the first periodic table that people widely accepted.
Francium, element 87, is so rare that it has only been photographed as light from tiny amounts.
